Yes, but dosing differs; exam focus is on adult dosing and principle.
faq.q: Can antifibrinolytics be used in children?

faq.a: Because benefit declines after 3 hours; early administration limits clot breakdown before massive blood loss.
faq.q: Why give TXA early in trauma?

exam: A trauma patient arrives 2 h after injury with oozing from surgical wounds – what lab test would you request to confirm hyperfibrinolysis? — D‑dimer; elevated levels indicate active fibrin breakdown.
Why is TXA avoided in a patient with recent deep‑vein thrombosis? — It can promote clot propagation by inhibiting fibrinolysis, increasing risk of embolic events.

In a malaria‑endemic region, a child with severe malaria develops bleeding gums – how does antifibrinolytic therapy help? — Malaria can trigger hyperfibrinolysis; TXA stabilises clots and reduces bleeding.
What is the main difference between TXA and desmopressin in managing bleeding? — TXA blocks plasmin formation; desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor to improve platelet adhesion.
A patient with chronic kidney disease needs antifibrinolytic therapy – what adjustment is required? — Use lower dose or avoid TXA; consider EACA with renal dosing or monitor renal function closely.
How would you manage a patient who develops signs of pulmonary embolism after TXA? — Stop TXA, start anticoagulation if not contraindicated, and arrange urgent imaging.

Explain why antifibrinolytics are valuable in low‑resource settings despite limited blood bank facilities. — They reduce transfusion need, are inexpensive, and can be given orally or IV without sophisticated monitoring.
ai.title: Antifibrinolytic Therapy
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Antifibrinolytics inhibit fibrin clot breakdown, reducing bleeding in surgery, trauma, and obstetric hemorrhage. They are inexpensive, orally or intravenously administered, and useful where blood products are scarce.

b: Key drugs: tranexamic acid (TXA) and epsilon‑aminocaproic acid (EACA)
Rapid onset, short half‑life, minimal renal clearance
sections.p: Antifibrinolytic agents block lysine‑binding sites on plasminogen, preventing its conversion to plasmin and stabilising formed clots. They are most effective when bleeding is due to hyperfibrinolysis rather than platelet dysfunction.

b: TXA binds to lysine sites, competitively inhibiting plasminogen activation
EACA is less potent but cheaper; both are renally excreted
sections.p: Hyperfibrinolysis occurs when excessive plasmin degrades fibrin, seen in major trauma, obstetric hemorrhage, cardiac surgery, and severe malaria‑related coagulopathy. Antifibrinolytics are given before or early after bleeding starts.

t.b: Is there ongoing fibrinolysis? – Elevated D‑dimer suggests active clot breakdown; if unavailable, rely on clinical bleeding pattern
Quantifies fibrinolytic activity – shortened time supports hyperfibrinolysis

b: Effective in malaria, sickle‑cell crisis, and severe burns where fibrinolysis is common
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, antifibrinolytics reduce need for blood transfusion, lower mortality from postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) and trauma, and are cheap to stock.

b: Distinguish hyperfibrinolysis from platelet failure – clot is soft, oozing, not petechiae
Know why TXA is avoided in active thrombo‑embolism
sections.p: Examiners test understanding of mechanism, indications, contraindications, and interpretation of bleeding patterns.

b: Using TXA in patients with known DIC with predominant thrombosis
Failing to monitor renal function in severe renal impairment
sections.p: Errors include giving antifibrinolytics after massive clotting has already occurred, ignoring contraindications, and confusing dosing intervals.

b: Avoid in active intravascular clot, recent thrombo‑embolic event, or severe renal failure
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause (e.g., control infection, repair trauma) and give antifibrinolytic early. Monitor bleeding, hemoglobin, renal function, and signs of thrombosis.

b: TXA ≠ desmopressin – different mechanisms and indications
EACA ≠ aprotinin – aprotinin is a serine protease inhibitor, not widely used
sections.p: Antifibrinolytics are sometimes mixed up with pro‑coagulants (e.g., vitamin K) or with desmopressin, which improves platelet function.

b: Rely on clinical bleeding pattern when labs are delayed
Consider malaria‑induced coagulopathy which can mask fibrinolysis
sections.p: Normal D‑dimer does not exclude hyperfibrinolysis in early trauma; low fibrinogen may be due to consumption, not lack of antifibrinolytic effect.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain or dyspnea after TXA – possible pulmonary embolism
Unexplained new neurological deficit – suspect cerebral thrombosis
Severe renal failure with rising creatinine after dosing
